catalog_quote: 3) LES TONS Le linda est une langue à tons. Il présente trois registres : haut [V́], moyen [V̄], bas [V̀], auxquels s'ajoutent deux tons modulés : un ton montant [V̌] et un ton descendant [V̂]. Pour ces derniers, seul le caractère mélodique, montant ou descendant, est pertinent. Le ton montant est généralement réalisé bas-haut; le ton descendant est réalisé haut-bas lorsque la syllabe suivante est porteuse d'un ton bas et haut-moyen lorsqu'elle est porteuse d'un ton moyen ou haut. ... b) Phonologie syntagmatique 1) FORMES CANONIQUES Les formes canoniques sont de type CV, CVCV, CVCVCV, CVV, CVVCV, CVCVV. Seuls les nominaux ou nominoïdes peuvent présenter également la structure à voyelle initiale : VCV, VCVCV, VCVCVCV. ... Il n'y a pas de structure syllabique fermée attestée (CVC). [Arom 2007, p. 2:] The present paper focuses exclusively on the Linda dialect, one of the most important linguistic varieties used by this group and one which is spoken by some 27,000 people living in the very heart of the Banda area. The Linda language consists of 32 consonants and 8 vowels. It presents no phonological opposition between short and long vowels, nor does it use accents. But each vowel is affected by a tone. The language has three registers —High, Medium, Low— and two “modulated” tones realized through a quick gliding from the low tone into the high tone, and vice versa.

new_statements.translation: 3) TONES. Linda is a tone language. It has three registers: high, mid, low, to which are added two contour tones: a rising tone and a falling tone. For the latter only the melodic character, rising or falling, is relevant. The rising tone is generally realised low-high; the falling tone is realised high-low when the following syllable carries a low tone and high-mid when it carries a mid or high tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Banda-Linda is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) and two contour tones (rising, falling); every vowel carries one of the five tones (p. 24). The reference grammar's phonological summary contains no statement about word stress or accent, and a full-text search of the whole book returns zero hits for accent/accentuation/accentué/tonique/prosodique; the 2020 SIL orthography précis (three level tones) is likewise silent on stress. No source for this language states where stress falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress statement at all). Tone-related remarks only: tones are 'd'une remarquable stabilité' (p. 29); internal vowels between C and l/r/v may be elided unless their tone contrasts with the following one (pp. 27-28).
new_statements.domain_note: Description of the Linda dialect of Ippy (Ouaka), the central variety of Banda-Bambari [liy], from fieldwork at Ippy and Bangui 1968-73; the phonological summary (pp. 24-29) condenses Cloarec-Heiss 1967 and 1969. Word-level phonology (canonical forms CV, CVCV, CVCVCV, VCV.; no closed syllables).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog band1344 'Banda-Bambari' = ISO 639-3 liy = Banda-Linda / Linda (Glottolog lists 'Linda' among its names; Lindaic subgroup lind1250). All first-hand material found is for the Linda dialect of Ippy/Bambari, i.e. the core of band1344 (Cloarec-Heiss 1986: fieldwork at Ippy; Olson 2019: speaker from Bambari; Dakpa et al. 2020: banda-linda [liy]). Two sources with explicit stress statements belong to OTHER Bandaic languages and must not be attached to band1344: Cotel 1907 (penultimate accent, p. XI) is 'rédigé dans le dialecte Togbo' (p. VI) = Togbo-Vara Banda, ISO tor, Glottolog togb1241; Sampson 1985 (stress non-contrastive, governed by tone and word shape) is Banda-Tangbago (Sudan).

new_statements.quote: 2. Tone and Stress 2a. There appear to be three main tone levels in these languages─High, Mid, and Low.1 Rising and Falling tones are common outside NDOGO-SERE, but seem for the most part to be the result of assimilation. Tone classes in Nouns and Verbs have been noted; tone also plays a grammatical role in Verb conjugation. ... 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here. Compare Eboué's BANDA spellings yaʋra (dog),2 yabru (goat), akblo (child) With Hackett's TOGBO renderings [examples not scanned]. 3. Word Shape ...

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'tonal' record (Cloarec-Heiss 1986: three registers H/M/L + two contour tones): Tucker & Bryan likewise give three tone levels for the group. It adds a stress remark absent from Cloarec-Heiss (stress affects vowel quality/length; penultimate syllable tends to extra shortness in Banda), but gives no stress placement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts any placement; statement is for BANDA at group level (Eboue's Banda, Hackett's Togbo), not Banda-Linda specifically. Snippet-level evidence only; a borrowed/in-library read of pp. ~105-110 would verify the page and the footnotes.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level sketch (Sere-Mundu and Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi together): three level tones (High, Mid, Low), rising/falling mostly by assimilation, lexical and grammatical tone. Stress is NOT located: the authors say only that stress often alters vowel quality and length, and that whereas Mayogo tends to lengthen the penultimate vowel, Ngbaka, Gbaya and BANDA tend to make the penultimate extra short, illustrated by Eboue's Banda spellings with elided penultimate vowels (yabru 'goat', akblo 'child'). No statement of which syllable carries stress in Banda; no statement that stress is contrastive.

new_statements.exceptions: none visible; footnotes 1 and 2 of the section and the Togbo phonetic examples were not scanned in the snippets. CAUTION: a snippet returned for the query 'Tone classes in Nouns and Verbs have been noted' reads '.. 2b. Stress, sometimes accompanied by a slight degree of length, seems to fall on the first syllable of a word Stem. The Noun Class Suffix is never stressed.' -- that passage belongs to a DIFFERENT chapter of the same book (languages with noun-class suffixes, e.g. the Mba group; its 2a ends 'have been noted.' not 'have been noted; tone also..') and must not be attributed to Banda.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan treat BANDA at group level inside their combined Sere-Mundu and Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi chapter, drawing on Eboue's Banda and Hackett's Togbo materials (no Linda-specific data visible); the catalog record and the verified statement held by the project are for Banda-Linda of Ippy (Cloarec-Heiss 1986). Banda-Tangbago (Sampson 1985) and Togbo (Cotel 1907) statements already held by the project are likewise sister varieties.

In two-syllable words, each syllable is stressed equally, regardless of tone.
